title: The bow
hook: back straight, hands on knees, glory to my Lord the Great

segments.voice: Yesterday: qiyam, the standing, the Fatiha answered line by line. Your line was stand and speak. Did you stand up straight before saying something that mattered? Day one hundred three.

Think about the last time you bowed to anyone. Maybe never. Maybe a small nod to a boss, a little dip of the head at a funeral. Most of us are shy of bowing. It feels like losing something. Now picture a man in the mosque in Medina, praying fast, up and down, done in a minute. He walks over to the Prophet ﷺ and says salaam. The Prophet answers him, and then says something he didn't expect: go back and pray, because you haven't prayed. Today: the bow, and what that man was missing.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU LAST BOW?` → `A MAN PRAYS FAST.` → `GO BACK AND PRAY.`

segments.voice: The bow is called ruku', from a root that means to bend, to bow down. After the recitation, the person says Allahu akbar and bends forward from the hips, hands on the knees, back level, head in line with the back. And there, usually three times, they say: subhana rabbiya al-'azim. Glory to my Lord, the Magnificent, the Great. A report in the Sunan says that when a verse came telling the Prophet to glorify the name of his Lord, the Tremendous, he said: put it in your bowing. Now back to the man in the mosque. The hadith is in Bukhari. He went back and prayed, and came again, and was told again: go back and pray, you haven't prayed. Three times. Finally he said: by the One who sent you with the truth, I don't know any better, so teach me. And the Prophet did. Among the things he said: bow until you are at rest in your bowing. That's the missing piece. There's a word for it, tuma'nina, stillness, settling. The body has to arrive in the bow before it leaves. Why does it matter? Because a bow that's only a dip is a gesture. A bow that settles is honest. It says, with the whole spine, that there's something greater than me, and I'm not in a hurry to stand back up. In the tradition, the only one a Muslim bows to like this is God. Not a king, not a teacher, not a parent. That's why it's honest: it's aimed at the one place it belongs.
screen: `RUKU' — TO BEND, TO BOW DOWN.` · `GLORY TO MY LORD, THE GREAT.` · `YOU HAVEN'T PRAYED. GO BACK.` · `BOW UNTIL YOU ARE AT REST.` · then, large: `A BOW THAT SETTLES IS HONEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow once, and settle. Stand, then bend forward from the hips, hands resting on your knees, back as level as it comfortably goes. If your back won't allow it, bow your head and shoulders instead. Stay there. Let your breath slow. If you pray, you can say it three times, subhana rabbiya al-'azim, glory to my Lord the Great. If not, count three slow breaths. Then stand, and sit. The bell holds the time.
Ruku'. The bow in prayer: back level, hands on knees, and still enough to be at rest. Today's word.
Your line: bowing is honest. Today, when you catch yourself rushing something that deserves care, slow down until you're at rest in it. Day one hundred three.

howItsDone: After reciting, Muslims say Allahu akbar and bow with hands on their knees and back level, usually saying subhana rabbiya al-'azim three times, and remaining still in the bow before rising.

fork.setup: you've prayed quickly, and the Prophet ﷺ has sent you back three times, saying you haven't prayed. what do you do?
options: pray even faster, to get it done
say: I don't know any better, so teach me
fork.reveal: the man asked to be taught, and the Prophet taught him, including: bow until you are at rest in your bowing (Bukhari).

original.note: Arabic: bowing, from a root meaning to bend or bow down.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslims bend over during prayer.
what it means: ruku' is a settled bow to God alone, with glory to my Lord the Great said in it.
what a scholar hears: the hadith of the man who prayed badly (Bukhari 757), the source for tuma'nina, stillness, as a requirement of each position.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 757 (the man told to go back and pray; bow until at rest)
Sunan Abi Dawud 869 (put it in your bowing, after 56:74)
Sahih Muslim 772 (subhana rabbiya al-'azim in the bow)
Qur'an 56:74 (glorify the name of your Lord, the Tremendous)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm. The Abu Dawud report linking 56:74 to the bow has been graded weak by some scholars; the script says 'a report in the Sunan'.
'The only one a Muslim bows to like this is God': prostration and ritual bowing to other than God are prohibited; ordinary courtesy nods are debated. A Keeper may want to refine the wording.
Hanafis treat tuma'nina as wajib rather than a pillar; the script doesn't get into the legal grades.
